lead: A potentiometer is a resistor with a sliding contact. Move the contact and the resistance between one end and the contact changes in proportion to displacement. Feed the track from a steady supply and the wiper voltage follows position. It is the oldest and cheapest displacement sensor: machine-tool slides, servo feedback, volume controls, and the inside of a Bourdon-tube pressure gauge. Its weakness is the load. The wiper must drive something without drawing much current, or the output bends away from a straight line.
prereq: You need the static characteristics — sensitivity, resolution and linearity — from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A potentiometer has a resistive track, two end terminals and a wiper that slides on the track. The track is wire wound on an insulating former, carbon film, or conductive plastic. Wire-wound tracks are robust but stepped. Film and plastic tracks are smoother and quieter. Linear types have a straight track of length L (mm). Rotary types wrap the track into a circle. Multi-turn and helical types give many turns for fine setting.

Connect the track ends to a supply V<sub>s</sub> (V). Let x (mm) be the wiper distance from the zero end. For a uniform track of total resistance R (Ω), the resistance from the zero end to the wiper is R<sub>1</sub> = R·x/L. The rest is R<sub>2</sub> = R·(L − x)/L. With no load, the output between wiper and zero end is a divider: V<sub>0</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·R<sub>1</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>) = V<sub>s</sub>·x/L = V<sub>s</sub>·α. The output is a straight line from 0 V at x = 0 to V<sub>s</sub> at x = L.

On a wire-wound track the wiper jumps from turn to turn. With N turns over the stroke, resolution is Δx = L/N, and the output step is V<sub>s</sub>/N. On a film or plastic track resolution is effectively continuous, limited by wiper size, contact noise and the readout electronics.

sections.h3: Loading error and the loaded divider

blocks.text: The straight law assumes no current leaves the wiper. A real load R<sub>L</sub> (Ω) connects across the output. Then R<sub>1</sub> is in parallel with R<sub>L</sub>, and R<sub>2</sub> is in series with that combination. The loaded divider gives V<sub>0</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·α / [1 + α(1 − α)·(R/R<sub>L</sub>)]. Write r = R/R<sub>L</sub>, the load ratio.

The extra term k = α(1 − α)·r is zero at α = 0 and α = 1. Both ends therefore stay exact: at x = 0 the output is 0 V, and at x = L the wiper is tied to the supply through zero series resistance. The term is largest at mid-stroke, α = 0.5, where α(1 − α) = 0.25. Loading error is ΔV = V<sub>s</sub>·α·k/(1 + k). For r = 1 at mid-stroke, k = 0.25 and ΔV = V<sub>s</sub>·0.5·0.25/1.25 = 0.1·V<sub>s</sub>. With V<sub>s</sub> = 10 V that is 1.00 V low.

The error is a fraction k/(1 + k) of the ideal reading. It is 20 % of reading at mid-stroke when R<sub>L</sub> = R. It is only 2.44 % of reading when R<sub>L</sub> = 10R. Keep the load at least ten times the track resistance, or add a high-impedance buffer. See Unit 6 for buffer amplifiers.

Linearity is good on a uniform film track, but wire-wound tracks are only linear on average; each turn is a step. Wiper friction adds a mechanical load. The wiper needs a small force or torque to move, and that force can disturb a light mechanism. Wear and dirt raise contact resistance and create contact noise, a random fluctuation in output. Vibration makes the wiper bounce. Life depends on track material, wiper pressure and speed. Wire-wound tracks last long but wear the wiper; conductive plastic tracks wear smoothly and are common in test and servo use.

Use a potentiometer where a cheap, absolute position signal is enough. Machine-tool travel uses a linear track along the slide. Older servo systems use a rotary or multi-turn pot for position feedback. A volume control is a rotary audio potentiometer. A Bourdon-tube pressure gauge can carry a pot: pressure bends the tube, the tube tip moves the wiper, and the voltage reads pressure. Some syllabi call this the variable-resistance transducer or the slider potentiometer. For bridge circuits, see Unit 6; for non-contact position sensing, see Unit 4, digital displacement sensors and position encoders.

figure.caption: The straight line is the ideal 10 V over 100 mm. The sagging curve is the same potentiometer feeding a 10 kΩ load: 4.00 V instead of 5.00 V at mid-stroke.

spec.aria: Two curves of output voltage against slider position over a 100 mm stroke; the loaded curve sags below the straight ideal line and meets it only at the two ends.

examples.question: A wire-wound potentiometer has a total resistance of 10 kΩ, is fed from a 10 V d.c. supply and has a 100 mm stroke. (a) Find the ideal output at 50 mm. (b) Find the actual output when a 10 kΩ load is connected across the output. (c) Find the loading error.
steps: Given: R = 10 kΩ, V<sub>s</sub> = 10 V, L = 100 mm, x = 50 mm, R<sub>L</sub> = 10 kΩ.
Fraction of stroke: α = x/L = 50 mm / 100 mm = 0.500.
Ideal output: V<sub>0</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>·α = 10 V × 0.500 = 5.00 V.
Load ratio: r = R/R<sub>L</sub> = 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ = 1.00.
Loading error: ΔV = 5.00 V − 4.00 V = 1.00 V low. As a percentage of the ideal reading: (1.00 V / 5.00 V) × 100 = 20.0 %. As a percentage of full scale: (1.00 V / 10 V) × 100 = 10.0 %.
examples.answer: The ideal output is 5.00 V; with the 10 kΩ load it is 4.00 V, a loading error of 1.00 V low, which is 20 % of reading and 10 % of full scale.
examples.check:
R = 10e3
Vs = 10.0
L = 100.0
x = 50.0
RL = 10e3
alpha = x / L
ideal = Vs * alpha
loaded = Vs * alpha / (1 + alpha * (1 - alpha) * (R / RL))
err = ideal - loaded
pct_reading = err / ideal * 100
pct_full = err / Vs * 100
print(f"{ideal:.2f}")
print(f"{loaded:.2f}")
print(f"{err:.2f}")
print(f"{pct_reading:.2f}")
print(f"{pct_full:.2f}")

traps: Quoting V<sub>s</sub>·x/L as the real output while a load is connected. The divider is linear only when R<sub>L</sub> is much larger than R; use the loaded formula whenever the load is within about ten times the track.
Mixing x and α. The formula V<sub>s</sub>·x/L needs x and L in the same unit; α = x/L is dimensionless. Putting 50 instead of 0.5 into an α formula gives an answer 100 times too large.
Saying loading error is largest at the ends. It is zero at x = 0 and x = L, and largest at mid-stroke, where α(1 − α) peaks.
Confusing resolution with accuracy. A wire-wound pot has resolution L/N from turn spacing; a film pot can resolve finer but still drifts with temperature, wear and contact noise.
Reporting loading error on the wrong base. State whether the percentage is of the ideal reading or of full scale; at mid-stroke with R<sub>L</sub> = R they are 20 % and 10 %.

quiz.q: An unloaded linear potentiometer has stroke L and supply V<sub>s</sub>. What is V<sub>0</sub> at x = L, and at x = L/2?
quiz.a: At x = L, V<sub>0</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>. At x = L/2, V<sub>0</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>/2.

quiz.q: Why is loading error zero at both ends of the stroke?
quiz.a: At x = 0 the output section has zero resistance, so the load is shorted and V<sub>0</sub> = 0. At x = L the series section is zero, so the wiper is at supply potential and the load cannot pull it down. The correction term contains α(1 − α), which is zero at both ends.

quiz.q: A 5 kΩ track has an 80 mm stroke and an 8 V supply. Find α and V<sub>0</sub> at x = 20 mm with no load.
Same 5 kΩ track, 8 V supply and 80 mm stroke, now at x = 40 mm with a 5 kΩ load. Find the loaded V<sub>0</sub> and the loading error.
A 1 kΩ pot feeds a 1 kΩ load from 10 V. Find the mid-stroke loaded output and error. Is this acceptable for a 1 % full-scale instrument?
quiz.a: α = 0.500, r = 1.00. V<sub>0</sub> = 10 × 0.500 / (1 + 0.250) = 4.00 V. Ideal = 5.00 V, error = 1.00 V = 10 % of full scale. Not acceptable for 1 % full scale; add a buffer or use a load at least ten times the track resistance.

quiz.q: Why does a wire-wound pot have a finite resolution while a conductive-plastic pot is called continuous? Give one practical limit on the plastic type.
quiz.a: A wire-wound track has N discrete turns, so the wiper moves in steps of L/N. A plastic track is a continuous film, so position can vary continuously. Practical limits on the plastic type are contact size, contact noise, wear, temperature drift and readout noise.

quiz.q: Give two causes of contact noise in a potentiometer and one way to reduce its effect.
quiz.a: Dirt or wear debris and vibration or wiper bounce. Use a sealed track, proper wiper pressure, filtering or a buffer; avoid operating near a mechanical resonance.

quiz.q: What is the main use of a multi-turn potentiometer?
quiz.a: Fine setting or measurement over many turns, giving high resolution for a given wiper travel.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pots still appear in volume knobs, joysticks, throttle pedals and trim settings because they are cheap and give an absolute d.c. output. Industry has moved servo feedback to encoders and resolvers, and non-contact magnetic or optical sensors avoid wiper wear. Conductive-plastic tracks dominate precision pots. Search next for conductive-plastic potentiometer linearity, wiper contact resistance noise, and potentiometer versus encoder for servo feedback.
